InfoQ Homepage Articles LLM Reliability Layers Under Test: Accuracy, Yield, and the Limits of Verification

Nov 10, 2026 15 min read

Clinical notes, incident reports, support tickets, and forum posts are prose, and a language model can read them. What it produces is not dependable. Ours was right about one answer in three on the task below and reported full confidence on two-thirds of its answers; wherever a wrong answer costs something, that is unusable.

We tested six layers, checks wrapped around the model, that each evaluate the model's output and flag what is wrong so that it can be put right: check each answer against something deterministic, send provable failures back to the model [1], sample it several times and vote [2], have a second model judge it [3], withhold what cannot be corroborated, and send the rest to a person. The theory we set out to test is that these layers are additive: each one catches errors the layers below it missed, so accuracy rises with every layer added. That assumption is what justifies stacking them at all. We ran all six on the same records, each priced, with the free check entered as a competitor. The theory did not hold. The layers sorted the answers by how far to trust them and corrected almost none.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog

Testing it needs a graded task, so we chose an annotated corpus: CADEC, the CSIRO Adverse Drug Event Corpus [4], 1,250 forum posts about two drugs, every adverse reaction marked as a span, the writer's exact words such as "rectal bleed", and given a SNOMED CT code. A gold answer for every mention lets us score each layer's verdicts instead of trusting them — and that assumes gold is the only right answer, which is not always true. Running one development document through the pipeline, the span "extremely sick" is gold-coded 213257006 |Generally unwell|; the model answered 39104002 |Illness| — an equally active, equally general reading that shares no wording with the span or with gold's own name. Naming either is a real answer; only one is scored correct. We did not build a CADEC system or tune for it: the aim was to evaluate open-weight models and measure how much each layer raises their accuracy, and CADEC is the instrument.

A supervised system does far better. CONORM [5], fine-tuned on 875 of CADEC's 1,250 files, reaches an end-to-end F1 of 0.72 under lenient span matching. Our zero-shot extractor, everything it returns, reaches 0.47 to 0.50 under the same matching on our development split, 0.39 to 0.43 span-exact. We are not competing with it: it needs those 875 annotated files, and still cannot say which of its answers to trust. Our held-out split was spent once: 60 documents, one run; every other number is development-side and says so. Two things would move the absolute numbers: the judge is small, and CADEC, public since 2015, is almost certainly in its training data. The comparisons between layers should hold.

The model is never asked for a code, and everything above it depends on that choice.

Figure 1: The pipeline, left to right, on one illustrative post (CADEC is non-transferable). Teal: a model call; grey: deterministic code. Each card shows what that step produces for the example; code appears for the first time in the last one. Image: the authors.

The model quotes each reaction; a retriever with no language model in it searches 227,554 keyword-to-code rows — every description in the SNOMED CT Australian edition of 31 July 2026 — embedding each quote with granite-embedding:30m, 384 dimensions, run locally, and showing the model a menu of the 20 nearest concepts to pick from. Codes are written as 271782001 |Drowsy|, SNOMED's bar notation, throughout.

We chose this shape by measuring the alternatives on 40 development documents, three cold runs each: recall the code from memory, name the concept and look it up, or pick from the menu.

Figure 2: F1 of the extractor alone under three ways of getting the code, one dot per cold run, with tokens per run and unparseable replies beneath. Image: the authors.

Recalling the code is not weak but broken: eight to twelve times worse than naming the concept. It answered null on up to 38 percent of records, and of the codes it committed to, 13 to 18 percent exist in no SNOMED release.

F1 is span-exact throughout: a wrong boundary is both a false positive and a false negative.

That is the extractor the six layers sit on. Before measuring what a layer adds, we had to know how much its output moves between runs of the same inputs.

Three identical runs of the unchanged extractor differed by four points of F1, at temperature zero.

We ran the extraction step three times, cold, on the same 40 documents. Two runs were byte-identical. The third diverged and finished with 98 correct mentions against the pair's 87. Grouped by mention, the runs give 233 mentions:

Where all three found the same span, they agreed on the code 84 percent of the time, so what moves between runs is mostly the reading, not the coding. We did not ask why those 22 were coded differently, and we should have.

The variation is a property of this model: four other families run three times each, llama3.1:8b, mistral:7b-instruct, qwen3:8b, and granite4:micro-h, returned byte-identical output every time. Our extractor, gpt-oss:20b, is the only mixture-of-experts model of the five and the only one that varied. Why, we could not settle: the diverging request, sent alone eight times, returns one reply; it moves only inside a full run. We kept it for its 6.5 extra points of F1 over llama3.1:8b.

From then on, every change was measured on three runs and reported as the range across them.

The two free layers did their jobs: the vocabulary check sorted the answers, and refusal withheld the doubtful ones, and neither changed an answer. Of the three paid layers, self-correction almost never fired, voting did not help, and the judge worked, but nothing read its verdict.

Development split, three runs of 40 documents; figures below are ranges across the runs:

Then we removed the three paid layers and replayed refusal: what it passed differed by one record on the first run and by none on the other two.

Voting and the judge's verdicts are good for diagnosis, not repair: a split vote marks an answer the model cannot reproduce, and a judge answering not on this menu marks a failed menu, not a failed pick. We did not use them that way, and should have.

Every verdict carries information. None makes the system produce more right answers, and they do not stack.

Figure 3: The first run's 230 records under each shipping rule. Dark green: right code on the exact span; light green: exact span, wrong code; light teal: right code, boundary off; grey: neither; amber: to a person. Dotted lines: the most the extractor found. Image: the authors.

Figure 3 reads each verdict as a shipping rule over the same 230 records. Three things hold.

First, any verdict raises the accuracy of what passes, because withholding is a layer's only lever. No rule ships more than the 88 right answers the extractor found, so every gain in accuracy is paid for in right answers held back. Accuracy alone flatters any withholding layer. Yield, right answers as a share of all records, cannot be flattered, so we report both.

Second, the price differs by verdict. ACCEPT is the most precise rule and the most expensive: moving to it removes 128 errors at the cost of 49 right answers and 177 records for a person, because the check can endorse only 32 percent of mentions whose wording matches the vocabulary. The menu-shown judge's verdict is informed rather than lexical, and it is the one rule whose F1 beats shipping everything, 0.420 against 0.397.

Third, the verdicts nest rather than add. Nearly everything the free check endorses, the judge endorses too, so a second verdict mostly confirms the first and can only remove records, never recover one the first held back; that is why removing the paid layers changed one record. Where every verdict agrees, the answers are almost all right; where only a vote does, almost all wrong. Each verdict is a different trade between errors, lost answers, and reviews; we recommend none.

The held-out split, run once, tells the same story. Before any check, one answer in three was right. Of those, the vocabulary check marked ACCEPT, five in six were right; of the rest, one in five. The check changed no answer; it only sorted them.

The domain knowledge was never missing. The model loses at reading, and nothing above it can see what it did not read.

Figure 4: Where the development split's 226 annotated mentions go through the shipped extractor, gpt-oss:20b, first run. Each bar is what the stage above kept; the dotted steps are what each stage lost. Teal: a model call; grey: deterministic code. Image: the authors.

Once a mention is found, the pipeline is reliable: the right concept reaches the menu for 93 percent of found spans and the model picks it 81 percent of the time. The loss is at finding. Nearly half the annotated mentions are never quoted as the annotators marked them, and none of the reasons are medical: single words go untouched where the annotator marked them, boundaries stretch — an extra adjective swept into a span the annotator left bare — and figures of speech are read literally, an idiom for exasperation coded as a nocturnal behaviour. Two domain-adapted models did not help: BioMistral-7B could not reliably return a parseable reply, and SapBERT as the retriever's encoder improved the menu and worsened the answer. A worked example and a denied-reactions rule did.

No layer can add a mention. Every layer above the extractor checks, re-asks, votes on, judges, or withholds an answer the extractor already gave; none can find a mention it missed. So the most any stack can ever get right is what the extractor found in the first place: on the held-out split, just over half the annotated mentions, a detection F1 of 0.521. The one way past that ceiling is a second reader: a different model family shown the post and the first model's spans, asked what was missed. We did not build it. Its additions would be proposals, needing the same measurement as the extractor's.

Four of the five lessons were held on other data. What changed is where the model loses, and where the free check can be trusted.

Seven further corpora [6–10], five model families; for each lesson, does the data agree?

The judge, the nesting of verdicts, and the diagnostic use of split votes were measured on CADEC only.

Every layer passed its own tests. The two defects that mattered sat between the layers and inside the metric.

The first was the unread verdicts. The second was the metric: voting overwrote codes without re-running the vocabulary check, so records shipped marked verified for a code they no longer held. Fixing that moved the held-out F1 from 0.204 to 0.204, because precision and recall cannot tell an unwarranted answer from a wrong one. We built six layers to decide which answers to trust, then scored them with a metric that cannot see the difference.

Both defects share a shape: a load-bearing fact recorded once, so nothing could disagree with it. Three checks built from that lesson, gatecheck, crosscheck and stagecheck, are reached from the repository below; stagecheck is a standalone package with no dependencies.

What transfers is not the layers but six practices, each earned above.

We set out believing that stacking reliability layers buys reliability. Measured end to end, they sorted the answers by how far to trust them and fixed almost none: worth a great deal, and not what we bought them for. The model reads. Almost everything else belongs to code, and one choice to you.

Code, ledger, decision records, and every figure's source. CADEC is non-transferable; we ship document IDs, never text.

La candidatura clamorosa di Teddy Riner alle elezioni presidenziali francesi del 2027 fa discutere soprattutto nel mondo dello sport. A commentare la scelta del cinque volte campione olimpico di judo è stato Ibrahima Konaté, intervenuto dal ritiro della nazionale francese a Clairefontaine. Il difensore del Real Madrid inizialmente ha preferito non sbilanciarsi, ammettendo di non aver seguito ancora nel dettaglio la vicenda: "Non ho visto nulla, davvero", ha scherzato Konaté davanti ai giornalisti. Il centrale francese ha però poi affrontato il tema più generale dell’impegno degli sportivi nella società e nella politica. "È un dibattito lungo. So che fa piacere ad alcuni e ad altri no, ma bisogna considerare che ogni sportivo ha una voce, ogni sportivo è un cittadino".

Konaté ha sottolineato anche la particolare posizione dei calciatori professionisti, spesso lontani dalle difficoltà quotidiane della maggior parte delle persone: "Ci troviamo in questa situazione grazie al lavoro e anche a un po’ di fortuna. Il difensore ha poi aggiunto un messaggio di responsabilità: "La nostra voce è importante. Però giochiamo a calcio prima di tutto e, quando parliamo, bisogna conoscere l’argomento e non parlare soltanto per dire qualcosa o per fare piacere a qualcuno".

Prediction: This Is Where SpaceX Stock Will Be at the End of 2027

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Artificial intelligence is driving rapid growth.

Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +5.81%), also known as SpaceX, got the valuation it was looking for when it went public in June. The initial public offering (IPO) was oversold, and the stock shot up at the open, reaching a market cap of $2.1 trillion. However, the market has lost its taste for the high-flying stock, which is down 17% from its first-day closing price.

The company is growing rapidly, and CEO Elon Musk has set high goals for the future. Is this a great time to buy? Let's see where SpaceX stock could be by the end of 2027.

SpaceX has three separate segments that also work together synergistically. The rocket-launching business is perhaps its most exciting venture, offering private space travel and working with enterprise clients such as NASA. It plays an important role in the Starlink satellite broadband business, bringing satellites into space, and Musk envisions mini solar-powered data centers for its artificial intelligence (AI) business, which was recently renamed superintelligence.

The company as a whole is growing fast, and each component plays a role. Total revenue increased 161% year over year in the third quarter, and it reported its first quarterly profit. With $32 billion in trailing 12-month revenue, it's still much smaller than the other large tech stocks that are worth more than $1 trillion, and it has that valuation because the stock is incredibly expensive, trading at 54 times trailing 12-month sales.

The space business increased 84% year over year in the third quarter, but it's still reporting a small operating loss. Starlink sales were up 69% year over year, with a $2.4 billion operating profit, and artificial intelligence sales increased 830%, reporting a $431 billion operating profit.

SpaceX sees artificial intelligence as its biggest opportunity, and it already accounts for about half of total revenue. If things continue to move in that direction, which is likely, SpaceX will be more an AI company than a space company.

It recently announced that it has committed to a $40 billion lease of Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs), the chips that power AI. It secured the funding through several financial firms and boasts that this is the largest GPU financing ever.

As of the end of the third quarter, SpaceX has 1.7 gigawatts (GW) of compute power, and management believes it could reach up to 3 GW by the end of the fourth quarter. To understand what that means, 1 GW is enough to power almost 1 million homes. Musk expects another 10 GW in 2027, and he thinks there's a chance it gets to 20.

Based on how much compute it can sell, Musk thinks SpaceX will have $500 billion to $1 trillion in revenue in 2027. That's quite a range, which makes it challenging to say where SpaceX will be a year from now.

Another angle to consider is whether the incoming Congress will curb AI development, which could slow SpaceX down. In any case, it's questionable whether SpaceX could grow that fast; the low end implies a 1,563% increase from today's trailing 12-month figure.

For the purposes of this exercise, I'm going to assume it can speed up, but not by that much. I'm also going to assume that the price-to-sales ratio will slow. Wall Street expects sales to increase 270% to $180 billion in 2027, and let's say the market is willing to pay 30 times sales, or just over half of today's multiple, for that kind of growth. If so, the market cap would reach $5.4 trillion, or triple today's value.

Jennifer Saibil has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Nvidia and Space Exploration Technologies. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

Big Walk Devs Issue Statement Over AI Usage

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

House House, the Australian development team behind indie hit Big Walk, has issued a statement via its FAQ page detailing a previously undisclosed use of AI "in the final stretch" of the game's development.

This comes following a "voluntary disclosure" as part of the game's submission for next year's IGF Awards. Earlier, a selection of IGF jurors issued a signed statement signalling their intention not to vote "for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity."

Specifically, House House says LLMs (Large Language Models) were used "sparingly [...] to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs." The team estimates that "well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code had anything to do with this usage," and stresses that "generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game."

While Steam requires a generative AI disclosure on its storefront, the platform "does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage."

House House provides an example of an issue that caused the game to "run 50% slower for around 20 seconds at sunrise and sunset":

"We researched the problem extensively, and we looked at the URP code ourselves, but we couldn’t find a way. Then, we were able to speak directly to an engineer at Unity, who asked around and ultimately concluded that what we wanted wasn’t possible. Finally, we posed the question to an LLM chatbot. After a few dead ends, it suggested a possible fix, and while we had to modify the suggestion extensively, it worked. This fix represented about 10 lines of code inside URP."

The developer goes on to say that this usage is "not an endorsement" of AI tools and that the developers "support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologise that Big Walk’s LLM usage may not meet their standards."

The lack of an internal AI policy was a "failure", according to the statement, and the team intends to "have a more comprehensive policy going forwards."

Here's House House's statement on its LLM usage in full (thanks, Aftermath):

In the final stretch of Big Walk’s development, LLMs were used sparingly by House House to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs. In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code—we’d estimate that well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game.

The primary use case for House House’s use of LLMs was to research, via chatbots, issues we encountered with third-party code. If you’re technically-minded, and curious, here’s an example. We needed to cull shadow casters by distance from the camera, but Unity URP only allows culling shadow casters by distance in camera forwards, so shadow casters behind the player were being rendered at an infinite distance. This made our game run 50% slower for around 20 seconds at sunrise and sunset. We researched the problem extensively, and we looked at the URP code ourselves, but we couldn’t find a way. Then, we were able to speak directly to an engineer at Unity, who asked around and ultimately concluded that what we wanted wasn’t possible. Finally, we posed the question to an LLM chatbot. After a few dead ends, it suggested a possible fix, and while we had to modify the suggestion extensively, it worked. This fix represented about 10 lines of code inside URP.

We originally wrote a version of the above disclosure as it was a suggested part of our IGF submission. We have not made any disclosure on Steam as the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage. We are posting this disclosure as it has become a matter of public interest.

This is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal. We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalisation of this technology, or its treatment as “inevitable”. We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologise that Big Walk’s LLM usage may not meet their standards.

Big Walk was developed without an internal AI usage policy in place, and we consider that lack of policy a failure. We will work to have a more comprehensive policy going forwards.

For further context, here's the earlier statement put out by a select group of IGF jurors, including Austin Walker and Sam Barlow:

Last month, House House published a separate statement explaining that the Palestinian-led BDS boycott against Microsoft is the reason the developer isn't publishing Big Walk on Xbox platforms.

House House was previously best known for its 2019 hit Untitled Goose Game. Big Walk launched in August 2026 to critical acclaim and reached one million sales in less than a week.

Andrade double helps FC Köln come from behind to beat RB Leipzig 3-1

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

To help deliver timely coverage of women's football, we may use AI tools to support content creation and editing. While we strive for accuracy and editorial quality, readers should independently verify important information.

FC Köln beat RB Leipzig 3-1 in the Frauen-Bundesliga on Monday 9 November, overturning a first-half deficit in Cologne. It was their third straight win over Leipzig, after a 1-0 victory in the DFB-Pokal on 31 October and a 1-0 league win in Leipzig on 21 December 2025.

Leipzig went ahead in the 20th minute without needing a finish of their own. Schmitz turned the ball into her own net to give the visitors a 1-0 lead.

Köln responded just before the break. In the 38th minute Andrade levelled from a Bremer assist. Two minutes later Leimenstoll scored the goal that proved to be the winner, set up by Imping.

Leipzig’s Schimmer was booked for dissent in the 41st minute. The home side went in 2-1 up at half-time.

The third goal arrived in the 57th minute. Degen provided the assist and Andrade added her second of the night, finishing with a rating of 8.92, the highest on the pitch, from 65 minutes of football. Degen was later shown a yellow card for a foul in the 63rd minute.

The numbers matched the scoreline. Köln had 22 shots to Leipzig’s 8, with 15 of theirs from inside the box, and built 2.29 expected goals against 0.52.

Finishing could have been sharper still. Fourteen of Köln’s attempts went wide, and they were caught offside 6 times. They also won 10 corners to Leipzig’s 6 and had 53% of the ball.

Leipzig did test the home goalkeeper. They put 5 shots on target and all 5 were saved, so their only goal came from Schmitz’s own goal.

Leimenstoll added 4 key passes to her goal and was rated 7.32. Bremer’s assist came from a player who already has 4 league goals this season, joint fifth in the Frauen-Bundesliga scoring chart.

Köln are sixth with 15 points from 9 games, a record of 5 wins and 4 defeats with a goal difference of 3. Werder Bremen and Bayer Leverkusen sit just above them on 16 points.

Leipzig are ninth on 10 points. This was their third defeat in a row in all competitions, following the cup exit in Cologne and a 1-5 loss to Bayern Munich. Before that run they had won three straight, against SC Freiburg, Mainz 05 and Blau-Gelb Marburg.

The turnaround in this fixture is marked. Leipzig won the meetings on 1 September 2024, 16 December 2024 and 6 September 2025, and have now lost the last three.

Both sides play again on Sunday 15 November. Köln travel to Nürnberg, who are 12th, while Leipzig host third-placed Eintracht Frankfurt.

PlugShare Gets A Major Redesign, Adds Dark Mode And iPhone Duo Support

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

PlugShare, the smartphone app that brings together the largest community of EV drivers in the world, has been redesigned to include new features and compatibility with new devices. Version 8.0, which is now live on the Apple App Store, introduces dark mode, a redesigned user experience, and a performance boost.

It’s the first time in the app’s 15-year history that dark mode has been available, and it’s all down to the PlugShare community, which has been feverishly requesting the feature for years.

“PlugShare has always been shaped by the drivers who use it, and we remain community-driven 15 years after our first app launch,” said Corey Davis, PlugShare Senior Director, Software. “The update is a near-total rebuild of the PlugShare app. We’ve redesigned nearly every screen using Apple’s latest design language, making it feel faster, fresher, and more useful for PlugShare users.”

The latest iOS app version adds support for the new iPhone Duo and improves a few user experience items. Switching between different tabs is now instant. Furthermore, users can open and zoom into location photos directly from the image thumbnails, and trips display the exact distance from the starting point and from the previous stop.

The Apple Watch app also got some love. Users can find nearby chargers directly on their wrist, and the smartwatch automatically applies the same filters set on the smartphone app, so drivers will only see chargers that are compatible with their cars.

Tapping on a location will show its Plug Score, the charging network, the connector types, and a small preview map. The list of chargers refreshes every time the user’s wrist is raised and the app is open.

Apple’s iPad also gets a rebuilt app that adapts its layout to the tablet’s screen size.

It’s not hard to spot that the latest PlugShare app is all about Apple devices right now, but Android users will get a refreshed experience, too. The company said it’s working on shipping dark mode and a Material 3-based design in early 2027.

PlugShare claims it’s the world’s largest community of EV drivers who contribute real-time check-ins, reviews, and photos. The service debuted in 2009 and has gradually introduced solutions for charging operators and car manufacturers, in addition to the charging map available for EV drivers for free. In 2021, Recargo, the company behind PlugShare, was acquired by EVgo for $25 million.

Anyone can create an account and use the app to find chargers from all operators. Some charging networks support payment through PlugShare and manage their locations directly, but in other cases, EV drivers are the ones who keep the locations up to date.

Il nuovo corso del Real Madrid targato José Mourinho ha portato importanti cambiamenti nella rosa e un aumento significativo dei costi. Dopo un’estate caratterizzata dagli arrivi di Ibrahima Konaté, Denzel Dumfries, Marc Cucurella, Bernardo Silva, Yan Diomande e Carlos Espí, oltre al rinnovo di Vinícius Júnior, il club ha raggiunto livelli record per quanto riguarda la massa salariale.

Secondo il portale specializzato 2Playbook.com, il costo complessivo legato agli stipendi di tutti i dipendenti del Real Madrid e agli ammortamenti dei contratti dei nuovi acquisti ha raggiunto quota 707 milioni di euro. Si tratta della cifra più alta mai registrata dai Blancos e di un valore vicino a quello del Paris Saint-Germain, società con i maggiori investimenti al mondo.

Nel dettaglio, 44,4 milioni sono destinati alla sezione basket maschile, che genera un passivo di circa 33 milioni, mentre altri 8,5 milioni riguardano la squadra femminile. Nonostante il peso economico della pallacanestro, la dirigenza guidata da Florentino Pérez ha deciso di aumentare ulteriormente i budget: 67 milioni per il settore maschile e 33 per quello femminile.

L’aumento dei costi, però, rientra nei parametri UEFA: la massa salariale rappresenta circa il 50% dei ricavi previsti per questa stagione, stimati in 1,405 miliardi di euro, cifra che sarebbe anch’essa un record nella storia del club. Una parte fondamentale arriverà dal nuovo Santiago Bernabéu, destinato a generare circa 420 milioni attraverso abbonamenti, biglietteria, sponsorizzazioni, museo, aree hospitality e anche eventi internazionali come una partita NFL.

A contribuire ai conti ci sono anche le cessioni, dirette o indirette, di diversi giovani: operazioni come quelle relative a Nico Paz al Como, Víctor Muñoz al Liverpool, Gonzalo García al Fulham, César Palacios al Fulham e Jacobo Ortega allo Strasburgo hanno portato circa 155 milioni di euro nelle casse del club.

The aggressive growth instructor was picky with her purchases to kick off the new trading week.

With stocks on the rise, Cathie Wood didn't have to do a lot of buying. As the founder and CEO of Ark Invest, she has a family of ETFs that is already deeply invested in many of the market's high-beta growth stocks.

This doesn't mean she didn't find buying opportunities in an otherwise buoyant day of trading. Ark added to existing positions in Nvidia (NVDA -4.27%), SoFi Technologies (SOFI +3.33%), and Scribe Therapeutics (SCTX +6.24%) on Monday. That was all the buying she did to kick off this market week. Let's take a closer look at all three of the stocks that Wood felt were worth buying during Monday's ascent.

The world's second most valuable company by market cap made headlines for all the wrong reasons over the weekend. Stories broke claiming that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an inappropriate relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

This is problematic for many different reasons, as the board investigates the matter. There are plenty of questions left to answer. Will Huang step down, forcing the board into an earlier succession strategy for one of the market's most prominent company leaders? Will Nvidia's chummy relationship with the White House come to an end, potentially slowing the government's cheerleading for AI adoption? If a Chinese spy gathered information about Nvidia and its business, would that make it more challenging to retain its customers?

Nvidia stock declined only 4% on Monday, a surprisingly mild reaction to some heavy news. The shares have fallen 27% since hitting an all-time high just last month, so there's that working in its favor. It also helps that its forward valuation is the lowest it's been in a long time. You can now buy Nvidia for a mere 11.2 times next fiscal year's profit target. Nvidia's stock has declined 5% over the past year. This is a stark contrast to a business with accelerating revenue and earnings growth.

The ceiling and floor remain high with Nvidia. On paper, it's too cheap for a company expecting revenue and earnings growth of roughly 90% when it reports its fiscal third-quarter results next week. In reality, Nvidia's wide margins don't seem sustainable in the long run. Any obstacle in the AI revolution -- and Huang will have some questions to answer next week -- can make Nvidia's forward financials look mortal.

The good news for SoFi investors is that the digital branchless bank operator rose on Monday. The bad news -- and it more than offsets the good news -- is that SoFi stock has plummeted 41% over the past year.

This should be SoFi's time to shine. Member growth has risen 35% to 17.1 million over the past year. Revenue rose 44% in its latest quarter. It's obviously encouraging to see the top line outpacing its user growth, a testament to SoFi's monetization efforts. That's not the end of the bullish case for SoFi. The bottom line is growing even faster, and it just raised its guidance when it posted fresh financials two weeks ago.

SoFi is trading at a reasonable year-ahead earnings multiple in the high teens. Rising rates may slow its personal, student, and home loan business. The bullish counterargument is that rising rates drive income investors to demand higher yields than conventional banks can offer. SoFi is currently offering up to 4.4% interest on savings accounts. It should continue to grow its audience at the expense of older institutions, but risks remain.

The biggest winner among the three stocks Woods was buying on Monday was Scribe Therapeutics. It rose 6%, but it's down 22% over the past year. Scribe is one of the many gene-editing stocks in Ark's portfolio. Its proprietary ELXR platform uses epigenetic silencing to suppress disease-causing genes without altering the actual DNA.

This is a long game, but its balance sheet is built to last. Scribe recently said it has enough cash to fund operations through early 2029. Time is on its side, as investors see if Scribe's science is also on its side.

InfoQ Homepage News Google Cloud Spend Caps Reach General Availability with API and Monthly Resets

Nov 10, 2026 3 min read

Google Cloud has made spend caps generally available on Cloud Billing Budgets, letting customers pause new usage of a service in a project once a monthly budget is reached, without deleting resources. The GA release adds an API, estimated live costs that trigger caps within minutes for AI services, and automatic monthly resets, but enforcement remains limited to Gemini API, the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Cloud Run, and Cloud Run functions.

A spend cap is a budget with enforcement attached: according to the documentation, when estimated spend on the capped service reaches the target amount, new requests to that service in that project are blocked, in-flight requests run to completion and are charged, persistent resources keep running, and nothing is deleted. Usage covered by committed-use discounts is paused along with pay-as-you-go usage, while Provisioned Throughput for AI models is never halted. Billing administrators and project owners receive alerts at 50, 80, and 100 percent of the cap.

The company changed three things between the July public preview and the GA release:

The limits are as specific as the features: a cap covers one project and one service for a calendar month, so folders, organizations, labels and multi-service budgets are out of scope, as are reseller accounts and subscription charges such as Gemini Enterprise seats. The estimate that drives enforcement is calculated at list price and excludes credits and discounts. Enforcement is also not instant: the documentation states that "any cost overages are billed as normal" and advises setting the cap "slightly below your absolute limit." Compute Engine, Cloud Storage, and networking are not among the eligible services, which means the cap addresses a runaway model or agent loop and not a forgotten GPU instance.

The narrower scope drew criticism when the preview expanded in October. On a Hacker News thread, one commenter who had asked Google for the capability a year earlier to control AI spend called the result "very crude, not granular like the rich IAM system," noting the four-product, month-only design. Another observed that Cloud Run had been added that morning, so the service list was still growing.

Developer Simon Willison argued in October that pay-by-usage services should default to hard caps, because coding and personal agents make it far easier to spin up code that calls paid APIs, and that "most businesses and individuals would prefer errors to a surprise $10,000+ bill." He cited Google's caps alongside a project-level spend limit in AWS's new account experience, which pauses the whole project and stops its resources when reached, preserving data for 90 days, and which AWS is rolling out to a limited number of customers. Azure's spending limit remains confined to free accounts and credit-based subscriptions; Microsoft states it isn't available for subscriptions with commitment plans or with pay-as-you-go pricing.

Spend caps pair with early anomalies, a daily baseline model that flags directional cost variances per service and names the top SKUs behind a spike, which Google positions as the detection half of the same control loop. Both are configured from the Budgets and Alerts page in the Billing console or through the Budgets API.

Google AI spots high blood pressure using ordinary watch sensors

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Google's smartwatch AI detected 65.8% of hypertension cases in a study, pointing to cuff-free screening using everyday sensor data.

Google researchers and medical collaborators have used ordinary smartwatch signals to flag possible high blood pressure without calibrating the watch against an arm cuff.

A study published in Nature on Nov. 5 suggests a way to prompt clinical checks during everyday wear, although the system missed about 33% of hypertension cases.

The AI identified 65.8% of participants with hypertension according to a clinical reference test (sensitivity), while it correctly screened 90% of those without the condition as negative (specificity).

The prospective, multicenter study followed 196 participants through seven days of smartwatch monitoring and compared results with 24-hour ambulatory blood-pressure monitoring. Participants had no known cardiovascular disease and were not taking blood-pressure medication, limiting how far the findings extend to people already receiving treatment.

The 95% confidence intervals were 54% to 76.3% for sensitivity and 83.2% to 94.7% for specificity.

The research system turns seven days of pulse and motion data into a screening score. Its detection rate leaves a substantial blind spot.

Of participants with hypertension on 24-hour ambulatory monitoring, 65.8% were detected and 34.2% were missed.

Of participants without hypertension on the reference test, 90.0% screened negative and 10.0% produced false alerts.

Screening can flag a reason for a clinical check; a negative result cannot exclude hypertension.

196 participants in a selected, risk-enriched cohort, without known cardiovascular disease or antihypertensive medication. Bars show conditional study rates, not predictive values for all smartwatch users. This is screening research, not a standalone diagnosis.

Reported sensitivity 65.8% and specificity 90.0% from the 196-person prospective study. JavaScript arithmetic: 100-65.8=34.2% missed; 100-90.0=10.0% false alerts. Bar lengths are proportional to these shares; no hypothetical patient counts. 95% confidence intervals retain reported precision.

196 participants in a selected, risk-enriched cohort, without known cardiovascular disease or antihypertensive medication. Bars show conditional study rates, not predictive values for all smartwatch users. This is screening research, not a standalone diagnosis.

The system, called AI-PPG-ACC-HTN, combines optical pulse-wave measurements with accelerometer signals.

According to Google Research's explanation, it aggregates those signals across days and combines them with the user's height to produce a probability of hypertension.

It does not report an exact systolic and diastolic blood-pressure reading. No personal cuff reading is needed to calibrate the smartwatch system, though cuff-based measurements remained the reference the researchers used to test it.

The waveform model was pretrained using 492,347 hours of unlabeled sensor data from 2,109 consenting participants.

The study supplement describes the prospective cohort as intentionally risk-enriched. In this selected group, 80.6% of positive smartwatch screens matched hypertension on the reference test, the measure known as positive predictive value.

The research involved Google Research, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School.

The authors describe a possible role for smartwatch screening in prompting formal assessment and confirmatory diagnosis using established cuff-based methods, with the watch prompting a clinical check.

PitchBook opens its platform to startups for free and debuts Origin deal sourcing service

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Private markets data provider PitchBook Data Inc. today opened its platform to startups for free at Web Summit in Lisbon.

Those that sign up have to share their financials. Some of that information will reach investors through the company’s new deal sourcing service, PitchBook Origin.

The launches come as more startups than ever are landing a first round. In the U.S., the 2021 record for first-time financings had already fallen by the end of September, PitchBook and the National Venture Capital Association found in their latest Venture Monitor report.

PitchBook credits artificial intelligence with part of that growth, since the technology has made companies easier to start. AI tools have also compressed investor diligence from weeks to days. Sourcing has not kept pace, the company argues, particularly where the signals are not public.

Free access for startups runs through a program called PitchBook for Startups. Founders who have bootstrapped or raised only from angels, grants or accelerators qualify as long as they are now seeking a first institutional round and can show at least a mockup of their product.

Once a startup has handed over its financials and details on its leadership team and product, its founders can use the PitchBook platform to research which firms are actively writing checks in their sector and stage. Investor research tops PitchBook’s own list of what founders can do with the access.

That founder data lands in a much bigger pool on the Origin side, where coverage starts at about 25 million companies and 250 million people profiles. Bootstrapped businesses and companies that have not yet raised money or announced what they are building are part of that count, and some 15 million of the companies are new to PitchBook.

Third-party data enrichment and PitchBook’s own machine learning models supply part of the coverage. PitchBook said it has not had founder-verified data at scale before.

Each company gets a score, and investors can tune relevance filters to their own criteria. Real-time alerts, saved searches and customer relationship management integrations are meant to replace the manual monitoring that deal teams do now.

Chief Solutions Officer Paul Santarelli said the missing piece for investors has been visibility into “the stage before a company raises, when the most important signals are the hardest to see.” Every company that joins the startup program and contributes verified information sharpens that picture, he said.

PitchBook “was once a startup itself, working to get in front of the right backers,” President and Chief Operating Officer Rod Diefendorf said. Founded in 2007, the Seattle company now serves more than 100,000 clients worldwide. Morningstar Inc. has owned it since 2016.

Startups can apply for the program now. Origin is available as a standalone product or as an add-on to the main PitchBook platform.

The Amazon Alexa Photo Frame made me cry — in a good way

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

The Amazon Alexa Photo Frame uses AI to smartly curate your huge collection of pictures, and present them in an orderly fashion. However, it's best for those who have an Amazon Prime subscription.

Lower resolution display than comparably priced models

Amazon Prime or Alexa+ subscription needed

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

I never thought a gadget would make me want to cry — least of all one from Amazon.

After unboxing and setting up the Alexa Photo Frame, one of the first images it displayed was a black-and-white picture of my father, who has been deceased for 16 years, feeding a squirrel.

I remember having the photo stored digitally somewhere, but it’s been several years since I last saw it. But the Alexa Photo Frame pulled it up, and juxtaposed it next to another picture of a squirrel clinging to a screen door. The Photo Frame also wasted no time digging up scores of photos of our family cat, who also died around the same time as my dad.

It was a very emotional first few minutes with this device.

But the Alexa Photo Frame also went on to deliver photos of my child playing, vacations and other happy occasions, which brought back more pleasant emotions.

While I have plenty of criticisms of AI and its use, this is one instance where I feel like it delivers something positive, and makes this one of the best photo frames I’ve ever used.

This might be stating the obvious, but if you want to get the most out of the Alexa Photo Frame, you’re going to need either an Alexa+ ($19/month) or an Amazon Prime subscription ($149/year), so you can use Amazon’s AI to its fullest.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The Alexa Photo Frame uses Amazon’s AI in one of the smartest ways yet. It combs through your entire library of images, and then pulls them up based on criteria such as the time of year, themes, objects, and events.

So, during the fall, you might be served pictures of pumpkins and leaves falling; in the summer, it might be photos of you at the beach.

While the Alexa Photo Frame only works in landscape mode, it does a clever thing with all the portrait photos in your library. If, for instance, you have photos of your child blowing out birthday candles over the years, it might put two of those images side by side, to show you the changes over the years. The photos of my dad and the squirrel was one example; another was two pictures of my kid potty training.

Or, if you want to go the more direct route, you can also ask Alexa to “show me photos of cats and kids,” and it will create a curated slideshow of all those images from your library.

Alexa+ isn’t perfect; when I asked it to create a slideshow of my daughter, a number of the pictures were of old ladies and some other random kids. However, it’s smart enough so that when one of these images showed up, I said “Alexa, that’s not my daughter,” and it went back through and edited the collection so those mismatched photos were no longer there.

Of course, the Photo Frame can act as a smart speaker. You definitely wouldn’t want to use it to play music, but you can use Alexa+ on it as you would any other Amazon smart speaker. And, should you not want it to listen, you can press the microphone mute button on the back.

Another trick with the Alexa Photo Frame is that you can attach short audio files to pictures, so if you’re gifting it to your parents, you can add a photo of your kids around a Christmas tree, with a voice note wishing them happy holidays. You have to tap the photo on the screen to hear the note, so it’s a nice extra, but I’m not sure how much it will be used.

Specs-wise, the Alexa Photo Frame isn’t the most impressive when compared to the best digital photo frames. The $229 Aura Aspen, for example, has a 12-inch screen with a much higher resolution of 1600 x 1200, and can be set up in portrait or landscape mode. The Lexar Pexar has an even crisper 2000 x 1200 display, and costs even less, at $179. And, the Alexa Photo Frame can’t play videos, which also make up a good portion of my phone’s library.

But neither makes curating all your photos as effortless — or as ingenious — as what Amazon does with Alexa+. For me, it’s solved the biggest issue I’ve had with digital photo frames and my massive photo library. How do I rediscover those old photos, and how do I make them show up on my photo frame without spending hours combing through everything?

‘But I think it’s my way of release from the game because it’s so intense, obviously.’

White’s return to the fold under Tuchel was eventful as he was booed in a friendly against Uruguay, where he scored and then gave away a penalty.

‘I think before the game, I was thinking, just don’t…not stand out, but just nice and easy, you know,’ he added.

‘Then I came on and obviously get booed. Then I score. Then I give away a pen. So it was obviously full of emotions that night, and it was a good night.

‘Everyone can do whatever they want. You know, it’s fine with me. Whatever they want to do, and I think just think about maybe not knowing the full story. And if they did, maybe they wouldn’t.’

White’s candid explanation for his actions and desire to rebuild his reputation holds no water with Waddle who was capped 62 times by England.

‘Listen, Ben White shouldn’t be in the England squad, that’s my opinion,’ the former Tottenham winger told iGaming.com.

‘He refused to represent his country. I’m surprised Thomas brought him back in, and I don’t get why he has.

‘There might be a shortage of full-backs, but when somebody turns down playing for their country, like Ben White did, to me that’s a lifetime ban. I’d say, ‘Forget it mate, on my watch you’re not getting back in’.

‘He’s not playing every game at Arsenal, so he’s a surprise inclusion to me. I think the England fans will show him what they think of what he did if he plays, because you don’t turn your country down and say, ‘I’m not interested in international football.’ I There are not many many players who would ever do that, and there are even fewer who have been able to resurrect an international career after doing so.

Jobe Bellingham has made England’s senior squad for the first time (Getty)

Defenders: Trent Alexander-Arnold (Real Madrid), Jarrad Branthwaite (Everton), Marc Guehi (Manchester City), Lewis Hall (Newcastle United), Ezri Konsa (Arsenal), Jarell Quansah (Bayer Leverkusen), Djed Spence (Inter Milan), Ben White (Arsenal)

Midfielders: Elliot Anderson (Manchester City), Jobe Bellingham (Borussia Dortmund), Jude Bellingham (Real Madrid), James Garner (Everton), Josh King (Fulham), Myles Lewis-Skelly (Arsenal), Declan Rice (Arsenal)

Attackers: Dominic Calvert-Lewin (Leeds United), Eberechi Eze (Arsenal), Morgan Gibbs-White (Nottingham Forest), Anthony Gordon (Barcelona), Harry Kane (Bayern Munich), Rio Ngumoha (Liverpool), Morgan Rogers (Chelsea)

‘Once you turn your country down, there should be an asterisk next to your name that means you will never get the opportunity to put on that England shirt again. End of story.

‘It’s all right coming out and saying, ‘Well, that was that time and this is now,’ but he knew what he was doing. If he didn’t want to play then, why does he want to play now? As I say, he’s not the permanent right-back at Arsenal.

‘Okay, he’s got that versatility where he can play centre-half as well. From Tuchel’s POV, I think it’s a very, very strange call-up for him to make and one that he probably doesn’t need to make.’

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

The revenue decline was driven mainly by lower digital asset sales amid a continued soft crypto trading environment and a higher mix of lower-margin stablecoin transactions, the company explained.

BitGo BitGo Holdings, Inc. (BTGO) saw a notable decline in revenue during the third quarter of this year, which it attributed to weaker digital asset trading activity.

According to its press release, BitGo reported Q3 revenue of $2.85 billion, down 50.9% from a year earlier and 34.1% from the prior quarter.

The revenue decline was driven mainly by lower digital asset sales, which fell 52% year-over-year and 35.2% sequentially amid a continued soft crypto trading environment and a higher mix of lower-margin stablecoin transactions. After direct costs, revenue was $37.3 million, down 32.1% from a year earlier.

Meanwhile, BitGo's net income rose to $44.1 million, up from $22.7 million last year. This growth was primarily driven by a $71.5 million unrealized gain on the company’s digital asset treasury. As of Sept. 30, the company held 2,399 BTC on its own balance sheet, valued at $200.4 million.

The company recorded an operating loss of $19.2 million and an adjusted EBITDA loss of $4.3 million.

"During the third quarter, we continued to strengthen BitGo's position as a leading institutional digital asset infrastructure platform," CEO Mike Belshe said in the statement.

Belshe cited the Go Network — the firm's institutional settlement and trading infrastructure — and its tokenized equity initiatives as some of the primary highlights in the quarter.

"We see significant opportunities to broaden access to U.S. equities through existing digital asset and stablecoin networks, while expanding the utility of traditional investment portfolios through on-chain settlement, collateral, and financing applications," Belshe added.

The company said normalized assets on the platform rose 32% year-over-year, reflecting continued institutional adoption when adjusted for price changes. It completed the acquisition of NYDIG's institutional trading business during the quarter and expanded off-exchange settlement connectivity, including with OKX. BitGo also repurchased $24.7 million of common stock under its $50 million authorization.

BitGo's NYSE-listed shares rose 4.94% to close at $5.10 on Monday and added another 2.9% in extended trading.

Lantronix: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Inventory was built to $31 million ahead of extended lead times, a move management tied to protecting supply for upcoming quarters.

On its first quarter of fiscal 2027 earnings call, held on Nov. 9, 2026, Lantronix (LTRX +5.52%) announced that first-quarter revenue grew 8% year over year to $32.4 million on strong demand for embedded edge computing. The compute hardware provider is expanding into high-margin software and specialized autonomous defense hardware, insulating its profitability from legacy network shifts. Three things management said stand out.

Lantronix is moving up the technology stack in unmanned aerial systems by consolidating discrete functions into single reference boards for autonomous drones and robotics. That hardware consolidation speeds design cycles for defense and industrial clients.

By acquiring Nero Global Tracking, a provider of fleet management tracking, Lantronix added high-margin recurring software revenue to its hardware base. Pro forma calculations, which show combined results as if the deal closed earlier, show services now exceed 10% of sales.

Demand from artificial intelligence data centers has constrained the availability of memory components across the embedded compute market. Management expanded net inventory to $31 million to secure system-on-module supplies, which are compact computing boards, and prevent delivery delays.

Demand across defense platforms and industrial vision is accelerating, and leadership is showcasing that momentum.

Federal trade compliance, hardware-software integration, and proprietary computer vision tuning give the business structural entry barriers. Leadership is watching component supply stability and pricing discipline while pushing for double-digit annual growth.

Know what you're getting each month with my comparison

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I don't know about you, but I am constantly hitting my token usage limits at the worst times. And it seems like whichever model I use, I get stuck much sooner than anticipated. Although AI coding assistants promise to take the hard work out of programming, it seems like the catch is that paying $20 a month doesn't mean you can keep coding for as long as you want. Unlike ChatGPT's unlimited free chatting, coding limitations are actually pretty strict.

Because I was so tired of hitting the wall, I decided to compare which subscription offers better value, particularly for someone who codes regularly but doesn't want to pay $200 a month.

Rather than burn through two subscriptions with unexpected coding challenges, I compared the companies' published usage policies, pricing and available independent research.

What I found is that neither company guarantees a fixed number of coding tasks for $20, and a major change coming to ChatGPT could make that decision even more important. Here's a closer look.

On paper, the subscriptions look very similar. ChatGPT Plus costs $20 per month and includes Codex alongside the regular ChatGPT experience. Claude Pro also costs $20 per month and provides access to Claude Code alongside Claude's chatbot.

Both subscriptions impose 5-hour usage limits and weekly allowances. The key difference is how those allowances work and how clearly users can estimate their remaining usage.

OpenAI publishes estimated message ranges for Codex models, while Anthropic explains that Claude's limits depend on factors including conversation length, model selection and task complexity. In other words, Anthropic remains completely vague about how and when you'll hit your limit.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Neither 5-hour limit means that much time of uninterrupted coding. You can use up your allowance before the window ends, which I have done nearly every day since subscribing.

One advantage Codex has is that OpenAI publishes estimated usage ranges for different models. I have found the company's current usage documentation helpful. Knowing what to expect is at least a starting point. From this, I have surmised that ChatGPT Plus users can expect approximately 5 to 45 local messages using GPT-6 Astra within a 5-hour window. Knowing this has helped me manage my token budget much better. For example, switching to GPT-6.1 Sol increases that estimated range to 15 to 160 messages, while GPT-6 Luna has an estimated range of 350 to 3,000 messages. Clearly, this is an enormous difference depending on which model you choose.

There are caveats, of course. These aren't guaranteed message counts, and a complex task involving multiple steps can consume considerably more usage than a simple request. Cloud tasks may also use more allowance than local messages.

Still, publishing these ranges gives users a better starting point when deciding which model to use.

Claude Code operates under a similar system, but Anthropic doesn't provide an equivalent universal table of guaranteed coding tasks for its $20 Pro subscription.

Instead, it explains that usage depends on the model, conversation length, features and complexity of the work. That makes it difficult — nearly impossible — to predict exactly how far $20 will take you with either platform.

There's another factor worth considering: how many tokens the assistants consume while completing tasks. A Zapier comparison cites a February 2026 benchmark involving a Figma-to-code task.

What matters is how much useful work gets completed before the subscription limit is reached. I find myself hitting a limit much sooner with Claude Code.

According to the comparison, Claude Code consumed approximately 6.2 million tokens while Codex used 1.5 million, a difference of more than four times.

However, Claude Code reportedly produced a more thorough result. That matters because lower token consumption doesn't automatically mean better value if the output requires more work afterward.

More recent data also reinforces how differently developers use these tools. An analysis from whoburnedmore published recently examined reported usage across an opt-in group of 229 developers over 30 days.

Claude Code accounted for 57% of observed tokens, compared with 35% for Codex CLI.

But it's good to note that this wasn't a controlled test of identical coding tasks, and the sample wasn't representative of all developers. It shows how much the participating developers used each tool, not which assistant is more efficient.

The takeaway is that token counts alone aren't enough to declare a winner. What matters is how much useful work gets completed before the subscription limit is reached. In my experience, I find myself hitting a limit much sooner with Claude Code.

Here's something anyone considering either subscription should understand. With Claude Pro, usage is shared across Claude's chatbot and Claude Code. This means, if you've been spending the morning researching, analyzing documents or working through a long conversation in Claude, that activity can reduce the allowance available for coding.

Anthropic confirms that usage across its supported Claude interfaces contributes to the same limits.

Codex has a similar consideration, although the structure is changing. Currently, Codex and ChatGPT Work share an allowance, with five-hour and weekly limits applying to Plus users.

But OpenAI says that starting in December 2026, Plus, Pro and Business subscriptions will move toward a shared ChatGPT and Codex usage allowance.

The company says usage will be measured in tokens, with consumption depending on the model and task. Instant chat won't draw from that allowance.

Neither subscription necessarily leaves you without options when you run out of included usage. It's all too tempting to pay for additional usage credits, which switch eligible requests to pay-as-you-go pricing after the subscription allowance is exhausted. But hopefully by understanding what you get, you won't have to now.

The important point is that paying $20 doesn't guarantee unlimited coding with either tool.

If you routinely work on complex applications, large repositories or lengthy agent-driven tasks, you should expect to encounter limits sooner than someone who only occasionally asks for a bug fix.

After comparing the published policies and my own usage, I'd give Codex the edge for users who want more visibility into their usage, particularly because OpenAI provides estimated message ranges for its different models.

Claude Code remains a compelling choice, especially for users who prefer its workflow or consistently get better results from Claude's models. Personally, I find it the more effective option the majority of the time for my projects. But if your biggest concern is paying for an assistant that suddenly tells you to come back later, both products require some planning.

For occasional coding, either $20 subscription could be enough. For more intensive work, the models you select, the complexity of your projects and your other AI activity can have a major impact on how quickly those limits disappear.

Sam Woods is TheGamer’s Senior Reporter. He’s been in games journalism since 2020 and has undertaken a variety of roles in that time. These have included roles such as SEO Editor, Managing Editor at DualShockers, and Global Head of Gaming, and he's also been seen on the BBC. He was promoted to the Senior Reporter position in 2025 following a series of high-quality reports and exclusives for TheGamer.

Since 2020, Sam has written over 3,000 articles and specializes in telling the stories of the people behind the games. He’s interviewed the biggest game directors, some of the industry’s top talents, told the stories of how indie games came to be, and spoken to players about what really makes them tick. He’s also interviewed some of the world’s biggest musical artists to find out how the medium has inspired their work, and TV and Film actors about their roles in video game adaptations. He even hosted a PAX panel in 2021 and made a documentary in 2024 surrounding the creation of a Disney game.

Alongside this, Sam focuses on breaking news. He got the scoop on Perfect Dark’s cancellation, provided context on some AI drama, and revealed that Lady Dimitrescu’s actress would love to step back into the character’s giant shoes. These articles have been picked up by the biggest gaming sites, including IGN, GameSpot, and PC Gamer. He also loves to dive into the numbers behind the games.

Sam’s journey in games journalism has taken him all over the world. He’s covered Gamescom in Germany, Summer Game Fest in Los Angeles, and Tokyo Game Show in Japan, each on three occasions.

He’s been learning Japanese since 2024 with the intention of identifying and translating Japanese-language news and bringing it to English-language audiences first, something he’s done countless times.

Sam’s first review was 2020’s Battletoads reboot, and he’s since reviewed games in The Legend of Zelda, Super Mario, and Pokemon franchises.

Late last month, the Nintendo Switch 2 was jailbroken for the first time. Modders, with the help of AI, found an exploit in a game called SmileBASIC that let them bypass many of the restrictions on Nintendo's latest hardware. It ultimately led to a heavily modded version of Mario Kart World, with characters like Cinnamoroll, Peter Griffin, and Hatsune Miku racing against the likes of Mario, Donkey Kong, and Dry Bones.

It was an early warning sign for Nintendo that its hardware wasn't as safe as the company must have thought, so naturally, they've moved to fix it, with today's Nintendo Switch 2 software update patching out the exploit.

Today, Nintendo released the Switch 2's Ver. 23.5.0 update. This update came with a range of changes seen below:

While gifting games is a fantastic addition, the patch notes don't mention that the jailbreak exploit has been removed. That was, instead, first spotted by OatmealDome on Twitter.

They claim that, at least for the time being, "Dumping and modding games will be impossible". They say there will be exceptions from some games releasing in the future, but for now, the loop is closed.

They add, "While game exploits like SmileBASIC and Civilization VII still exist, it is no longer possible to 'escape' the game starting with 23.5.0. This effectively means that the capabilities of homebrew are locked to whatever the game can do already."

It's no surprise that Nintendo got on top of this one, especially given the situation it's facing with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on PC.

Is Bitcoin’s [BTC] growing negative correlation to other risk assets becoming a key headwind?

It has been less than 48 hours since the most recent crypto wipeout resulted in over $1 billion in liquidations, pushing Bitcoin close to $70k, and sending market sentiment into extreme fear. While Bitcoin continues to trade below $75k, the S&P500 has risen by over 2%, pointing to stronger resilience despite the ongoing FUD.

This growing disparity raises questions about Bitcoin’s performance as a macro hedge this cycle. Notably, Peter Schiff shares his view. As his post below highlights, the long-time Bitcoin critic has warned of a deeper BTC correction, citing its underperformance compared to other risk assets. Even precious metals such as gold and silver have gained over 2%, further widening the performance gap.

Against this backdrop, positioning for further downside is starting to make more sense.

According to CoinGlass data, Bitcoin’s long/short ratio is showing bearish signs as it fell back from a 3-month high of 1.4 on the 7th of November, indicating traders are returning to shorting their positions, signaling weaker confidence in BTC’s near-term recovery. The key takeaway? There is no downside liquidity left to be hunted. The recent $1 billion liquidation event has wiped out almost all long-side liquidity.

This can be considered a great chance for bulls to recover. If Bitcoin remains above $75k and accumulation continues, then both early and late short positions could come under pressure. In fact, one analyst highlighted over $11 billion in short liquidity clustered around $87k.

Interestingly, bulls already seem to be positioning for this potential move.

Despite the scale of the recent wipeout, market sentiment is already showing signs of recovery.

The Crypto Fear & Greed Index shows that sentiment has improved by four points to 32. This indicates that selling pressure may be losing steam and that confidence is returning. Notably, institutional activity is also adding to this shift. As on-chain data reported, MSTR recently bought an additional 1,036 BTC.

To add to this, MARA Holdings has announced a Q3 net profit of $634.4 million, up from $123.1 million in the previous year. This is backed up by Santiment data showing a distinct increase in accumulation between retail and mid-sized holders. In the past two weeks the market has seen an increase of 1-10 BTC wallets by 10,076 BTC and 10-100 BTC wallets by 4,131 BTC.

In short, just because BTC has failed to outperform other assets does not mean that the rally is dying.

Despite macro uncertainty and bearish positioning being a key factor, there are clear signs of increasing institutional exposure and accumulation across wallet classes. If Bitcoin can hold above $75k, the current divergence could turn into a potential bear trap, with the $87k short-liquidity cluster becoming the next major upside target.

Bitcoin is lagging traditional markets, but institutional buying and whale accumulation remain strong.

If Bitcoin holds $75k, a short squeeze could push prices toward $87k.

Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Long-context training — including pretraining and post-training, has become a foundation of frontier AI models. Longer native sequence lengths give large language models (LLMs) the working memory to read a whole code repository or ingest hours of video, and reason through multi-step agentic tasks. In three years, context windows have grown from 128K–200K tokens to 1M–2M, and models trained toward 10M tokens are arriving. Training at those lengths, not just serving them, is where the system limits show up.

In particular, efficient training at multi-million-token sequence lengths runs into the following bottlenecks:

Today, we are excited to announce long-context training support in MaxText, Google Cloud's open-source JAX training framework. MaxText enables this by supporting four context-parallel strategies on Cloud TPU: All-gather, A2A (DeepSpeed Ulysses), P2P (Ring Attention), and the A2A + P2P hybrid (Unified Sequence Parallelism, or USP), combined with load balancing and sequence packing. All four use the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel. Combined with the 3D inter-chip interconnect (ICI) ( supported on TPUs such as TPU 5p or TPU 7 (Ironwood) ), this lets one sequence span an entire slice while communication overlaps compute and memory per chip stays flat. In our benchmarks, Llama 3.1 8B (25 head dim, 16 query heads) demonstrates exceptional long-context efficiency, achieving 70% Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) on TPU 5p for sequence lengths up to 4 million tokens. Across both TPU 5p and TPU 7, context can be seamlessly extended to 14 million tokens—with TPU 7 consistently maintaining 50% MFU across all sequence scales below 6 million tokens.

This functionality is available today in MaxText v0.2.4(doc).

Context parallelism splits a long sequence across chips, so no chip holds the activations of the whole sequence. Context parallelism can be combined with data and tensor parallelism, and the smallest context-parallel size that fits your sequence in HBM is usually the right one. This also holds for sparser attention variants which cut attention compute but not the activations of every other layer.

Attention is the one global operation where every token needs the keys and values of every preceding token, so each context parallel strategy has to bring those keys and values back together. Each makes a different tradeoff between memory (how much KV a chip holds), communication (how much moves per layer, and whether it overlaps compute), and model shape (how many attention heads to split).

All-gather: Each chip keeps its chunk of the sequence and, at every layer, gathers the keys and values from every other chip. It is the simplest option. However, because causal masking causes later tokens to attend to larger prefixes, All-gather requires balancing compute load across devices.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

All-to-All (Ulysses): Gathering keys and values makes every chip hold the whole sequence, so attention memory never shrinks no matter how many chips you add. All-to-All changes what each chip owns instead. Attention is independent across heads but not across tokens, so the head axis is free to shard and the token axis is not. An All-to-All before attention rotates the sharding from one onto the other: each chip gives up the heads it is not responsible for and receives the tokens it was missing for the heads it keeps, ending up with the full sequence for a few heads instead of a few tokens for all heads. This is also why Ulysses does not need token load balancing. Attention then runs as ordinary single-chip attention with standard kernels, and a second All-to-All rotates the output back. KV per chip shrinks by the context-parallel factor, but you cannot split across more chips than the model has heads — and tensor parallelism shards that same dimension, so TP × CP is capped by the head count (under GQA, by the KV heads: eight for Llama 3 8B). The all-to-all itself, though, does not overlap with compute — attention cannot start on a partial sequence, so every chip waits for data from every other chip before any of them begins.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

P2P (ring attention): Ulysses' ceiling is the head count; ring attention removes it by never leaving the token axis. Keys and values never materialize in full. KV chunks travel around a ring of chips one hop at a time, neighbor to neighbor. Each chip attends its queries to the chunk it holds while the next one is in flight, and merges the partial results as it goes. A chip holds its own chunk and one visiting chunk, never the full sequence, and the communication overlaps compute. However, dividing attention computation into smaller chunks can reduce local kernel efficiency, and unlike All-to-All Ulysses, ring attention requires explicit load balancing.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

A2A + P2P (USP): A2A + P2P (USP): Neither strategy scales on its own — All-to-All stops at the head count, and a long ring accumulates hops while thinning the overlap that makes it work. Unified sequence parallelism composes them on two axes of the chip mesh, so the context-parallel degree becomes the product of the two: All-to-All along one axis, sized at or below the KV-head count, and a ring along the other to extend past it. Because each All-to-All group has already pooled its tokens, a ring step now carries a chunk larger by the All-to-All factor, and the ring is correspondingly shorter — more compute per hop to hide the transfer behind, and fewer hops to accumulate latency and causal imbalance. On Cloud TPU the two map onto two axes of the slice's chip mesh.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

These strategies cover the attention variants in today's major models, from multi-head and grouped-query attention to DeepSeek-style multi-head latent attention.

Splitting the sequence only pays off if the attention compute on each chip stays efficient. All four strategies run on Splash Attention, the block-sparse flash attention kernel from Tokamax, Google's open-source library of TPU kernels. It skips fully masked blocks and handles packed sequences without padding. P2P calls it once per ring step, on the local queries and the KV chunk that has just arrived, while the transfer for the next step runs underneath, in the forward and backward pass alike. Each chip does the same fused, block-level work it would do without context parallelism, with the communication hidden behind it.

P2P (Ring Attention) is the primary workhorse for very long-context training, whereas All-Gather is the standard baseline for most other cases where the KV can fit. These are the primary CP strategies to use in practice. We compare how far each can push context length on a fixed 64-chip TPU 5p slice with Llama 3.1 8B (256 head dim, 16 query heads) , and measure their MFUs. In ideal settings where both strategies can have large enough chunks (S/CP) and local batch size - the two major variables driving MFU on TPU 5p, we observe that P2P can outperform All-Gather almost every context length from 64K to 14M tokens, where communication becomes mostly hidden with the Ring circular transport schedule.

TPU v7x (Ironwood) takes the same recipe further. With twice the HBM per chip, P2P training of 14M tokens on 64 TPU 7 chips reached 48.7% Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) compared to 37.1% on TPU 5p. We observed that ring attention performs better than other context parallelism strategies -- e.g. Ulysses and USP –- on TPU 7 chips.

The choice of context parallelism strategy depends mostly on whether the gathered KV fits in HBM, and on how many KV heads the model has:

For all CP strategies, when you run low on memory: Offload before you recompute. MaxText can move saved activations, optimizer states, and parameters to host memory tensor by tensor. At long context lengths, these transfers are hidden behind compute, making offloading effectively free. Offload attention outputs first, followed by optimizer states, layer inputs, parameters, and finally remat as a last resort. MFU stays flat through the offload steps while all-gather falls off and eventually stops fitting. For more details, see the remat tuning guide.

Looking ahead, we see two natural extensions. The first is broader model coverage. Models that mix sliding-window and global layers, such as Gemma, would run the window layers with a short exchange between neighboring chips while the global layers use the ring. We also plan to support linear attention mechanisms such as Gated Delta Net (GDN) and Kimi Delta Attention (KDA). The second is performance, with further tuning of the Tokamax kernels and the P2P backward pass to narrow the remaining gap to all-gather at short context, and recipes by model and context length for TPU 5p and 7 chips.

Context parallelism is available today in MaxText v0.2.4 on PyPI, the corresponding Docker images and on GitHub main. Sample recipes are available here for TPU 7 and TPU 5p. Pick a strategy with context_parallel_strategy (ring, ulysses, or usp), set the context-parallel size, and keep the rest of your run the same. The sharding guide has the flags and constraints for each strategy, and the release notes link to the pull requests behind this work. We can't wait to see what you train.

What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
